pointers.sentence: `django/contrib/auth/forms.py` holds the forms under the login and password views and the admin: `AuthenticationForm`, which checks a username and a password with `authenticate`; `SetPasswordMixin`, which checks a new password typed twice and sets it, and the forms built on it; and `UserChangeForm`, which shows the stored hash and never a password.

`AuthenticationForm` takes its user model from `get_user_model` when the module is imported, and the password forms are handed their user, so these serve any subclass of `AbstractBaseUser`; the creation and change forms are model forms of `User`, which a project with its own user model rewrites or extends (`docs/topics/auth/customizing.txt`).

A value longer than the field's `max_length` is left alone: normalizing, says the comment, can lengthen a string but never shorten it, so such a value fails anyway, and it is slow enough on Windows to serve a denial of service (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:UsernameField.to_python`).

Its username field is called `"username"` whatever the user model calls its own: `AuthenticationForm.__init__` gives it the `max_length` of the field that `USERNAME_FIELD` names, or 254 where that has none, and its verbose name as the label if none is set (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:AuthenticationForm.__init__`).
`AuthenticationForm.get_user` returns the user kept, or `None`, and `LoginView` passes it to `login` (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:AuthenticationForm.clean`).

`confirm_login_allowed` refuses a user whose `is_active` is false, code `"inactive"`, but under the default backend it never meets one: `ModelBackend.user_can_authenticate` refuses such a user first, and the inactive user with the right password is told what everyone is told (`django/contrib/auth/backends.py:ModelBackend.user_can_authenticate`).

The method decides only under a backend that lets inactive users through, such as `AllowAllUsersModelBackend`, as the documentation says, and then only for a right password (`docs/topics/auth/default.txt`):

The admin's `AdminAuthenticationForm` extends `confirm_login_allowed` to refuse a user who is not staff (`django/contrib/admin/forms.py:AdminAuthenticationForm.confirm_login_allowed`) ([The admin](../admin.md)).

It checks the match in `clean` and runs the validators in `_post_clean`, after `BaseModelForm._post_clean` has copied the cleaned values onto the new user, as its comment says; so `UserAttributeSimilarityValidator` compares the password with the username being chosen (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:BaseUserCreationForm._post_clean`).

`UserCreationForm.clean_username` adds a match that ignores case (`"username__iexact"`), and files the model's message for a duplicate, from `Model.unique_error_message`, through `BaseModelForm._update_errors`; it then returns nothing, so `cleaned_data` holds `None` for the username, and the model's own check passes over a field with an error (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:UserCreationForm.clean_username`).
The documentation's reason is confusion between similar usernames (`docs/topics/auth/default.txt`).
The base form has only the model's check, an exact match, which on the example's SQLite database finds no "Nora" (`django/db/models/base.py:Model._perform_unique_checks`):

False, nothing is checked and saving calls `AbstractBaseUser.set_unusable_password`; true, an empty password field is refused as `"required"`, the fields being optional where the radio is offered, and `SetPasswordMixin` does the rest (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:SetUnusablePasswordMixin.validate_passwords`).

Those forms are the admin's: `AdminUserCreationForm`, a `UserCreationForm` with the radio, and the `AdminPasswordChangeForm` of `django/contrib/auth/forms.py`, which offers it only for a user whose password is usable (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:AdminPasswordChangeForm.__init__`) ([The admin](../admin.md)).

A disabled field cleans its initial value whatever was posted, so the form writes the stored hash back as it was ([A form field: the base class](../forms/fields.md)) (`django/contrib/auth/forms.py:ReadOnlyPasswordHashField`).

Its widget, `ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget`, draws `"auth/widgets/read_only_password_hash.html"`, which calls the tag `render_password_as_hash`: "No password set." for an empty or unusable string, "Invalid password format or unknown hashing algorithm." where finding the hasher or reading the string raises `ValueError`, otherwise what `BasePasswordHasher.safe_summary` gives for the hasher `identify_hasher` finds, for PBKDF2 the salt and the hash starred after six characters (`django/contrib/auth/templatetags/auth.py:render_password_as_hash`).

A button follows, "Reset password", or "Set password" with no usable password, linking to `"../password/"`, which from a user's change page in the admin is the password page that `UserAdmin.get_urls` adds (`django/contrib/auth/admin.py:UserAdmin.get_urls`):
